nameStory: Indian tobacco gets its name because Native Americans traditionally smoked this plant for respiratory ailments, using it similarly to how Europeans used true tobacco. The alternate name "puke weed" comes from one of its more unpleasant effects - the plant contains compounds that can cause nausea and vomiting if consumed.
description: Indian tobacco is a slender annual wildflower that grows 1-4 feet tall with a single, unbranched stem. It produces tiny pale blue to white flowers arranged in a long, spike-like cluster at the top of the plant. The small, oval leaves alternate up the stem and have toothed edges. Despite its name, it's not related to true tobacco but belongs to the bellflower family.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pale blue, lavender, or white tubular flowers arranged in a long terminal spike. Each flower is only about 1/4 inch long with an irregular, two-lipped shape that looks almost like a tiny snapdragon.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves with serrated (toothed) edges that alternate up the stem. Lower leaves are larger and may be slightly fuzzy to the touch, while upper leaves become progressively smaller.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a single, unbranched stem from 1-4 feet tall. The plant has a distinctive upright, wand-like appearance with the flower spike making up much of the upper portion.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, inflated seed capsules that give the plant part of its scientific name 'inflata.' The capsules are round and balloon-like when mature, containing numerous tiny seeds.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: The stem is typically unbranched, smooth or slightly hairy, and often has a reddish tinge. When broken, it may release a slightly milky sap with an acrid smell.

habitat: Indian tobacco thrives in disturbed soils and open areas throughout New England, including roadsides, old fields, woodland edges, and clearings. It prefers sandy or gravelly soils and can often be found in areas that have been recently disturbed by human activity. You'll commonly spot it in sunny to partially shaded locations from sea level to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes of toothed leaves close to the ground. The distinctive single stem begins to elongate in late spring.
seasonality.summer: The characteristic flower spike develops and blooms from bottom to top throughout mid to late summer. This is the best time for identification when the pale blue flowers are most visible.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and the inflated seed capsules become prominent. The entire plant often takes on a brownish color as it prepares to die back for winter.
seasonality.winter: As an annual, the plant dies completely, leaving only dried stems and scattered seeds. Look for the distinctive dried flower spikes which may persist into early winter.

funFact: Indian tobacco contains the same addictive compound (nicotine) as regular tobacco, but in much higher concentrations - making it potentially dangerous to handle or consume, despite its historical medicinal uses.
confusionNotes: Indian tobacco is most often confused with other spike-flowered plants like plantains or speedwells, but its distinctive inflated seed capsules and pale blue tubular flowers set it apart. Remember: if the flowers look like tiny blue snapdragons on a spike, you've likely found Indian tobacco.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name, Indian tobacco is completely unrelated to true tobacco (Nicotiana species) and belongs to the bellflower family instead. However, both plants do contain nicotine, which explains why Native Americans found similar uses for them. Modern foragers should avoid this plant entirely due to its toxic properties.
compareHints: Unlike its showier relatives cardinal flower (bright red) and great blue lobelia (deep blue), Indian tobacco has much smaller, paler flowers. While cardinal flower and great blue lobelia prefer wet areas, Indian tobacco thrives in dry, disturbed soils. The inflated seed capsules are unique among the New England lobelias and help distinguish it from its cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Cardinal flower stands out dramatically from its lobelia relatives—while great blue lobelia produces similar tubular flowers in blue, and Indian tobacco has tiny pale flowers, only cardinal flower blazes in brilliant red.
Among New England's lobelias, great blue lobelia is easily distinguished by its brilliant blue color and robust size.
Unlike its showy red cousin cardinal flower or the tall blue spikes of great blue lobelia, water lobelia is the only member of the lobelia family that lives completely underwater.
Among New England's lobelias, pale-spiked lobelia is the wallflower of the family with its subtle white or pale blue flowers.
Kalm's lobelia is much smaller and more delicate than its showy relatives like cardinal flower (bright red) or great blue lobelia (deep blue, much larger).
Garden lobelia is much smaller and more delicate than its New England native relatives like cardinal flower and great blue lobelia, which are tall, upright wetland plants.

Unlike its native Lobelia relatives such as cardinal flower or great blue lobelia which grow as upright leafy stems with showy flower spikes, matted pratia is a tiny mat-forming groundcover with individual star-shaped flowers.
Nuttall's lobelia is much smaller and more delicate than its famous relatives like cardinal flower (bright red) or great blue lobelia (deep blue and tall).
